newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Puerto Rico lawmaker expands breast feeding battle.
newsitem.headline: Puerto Rico lawmaker expands breast feeding battle.

text.p: A Puerto Rican lawmaker who this year filed legislation to win breast-feeding rights in the workplace is expanding the battle for mother's milk.

Representative Victor Garica San Inocencio filed three bills in the House of Representatives on Wednesday to encourage breast feeding, saying manufacturers of infant formula are damaging the health of women and infants by encouraging the use of formulas instead of breast milk.
"Breast-feeding is disappearing from our culture," Garcia said. "The mother's milk is the best, most nutritious food for our children."
One bill would force manufacturers to put a warning on their labels that "breast milk is the best nourishment for a baby, preventing many childhood diseases."

Garcia, a member of the Puerto Rico Independence Party, said fewer than one in 10 lactating mothers in Puerto Rico breast-feed through the first year of a baby's life, despite studies showing breast-feeding can cut down on ear infections, respiratory ailments and other childhood illnesses.
Puerto Rico reported about 62,000 live births last year and "every one of these women was subjected to a great publicity machine trying to convince them not to breast-feed."

"The companies that sell formula have, through sophisticated marketing techniques, used public health issues to convince people that what is sold in a glass jar is nutritionally equal to mother's milk," he said.
Another of Garcia's bills would bar use of public funds in activities promoting the use of infant formula, effectively preventing public hospitals from distributing formula for free.

The third would prevent hospitals from restricting mothers' access to infants. Garcia said some hospitals refuse to set up regular breast-feeding schedules, claiming they do not have adequate staff to do so.

Earlier this year Garcia submitted a bill that would force businesses to give lactating mothers time off during the work day to breast-feed. The bill passed the House in July and will be up for a vote in the Senate when the legislative session begins Aug. 18.
